title: Origins of Judaism
summary: Israelites remained henotheists, focusing on one supreme god among many, through the time of the Judges and the Kingdom of Israel. The Kingdom of Judah survived until 586 BCE, when the Babylonians conquered it, Jerusalem fell, and its people went into exile. Those who gave the Hebrew scriptures their final form held an ethical monotheistic perspective, and tried to impose it on their older source material.

uncertainty.note: Traditional and archaeological chronologies place the emergence of the United Monarchy and early Kingdom of Israel around 1080–931 BCE; the Babylonian destruction took place in 586 BCE and the Second Temple was consecrated c. 516 BCE.

as_recorded.value: The Israelites remained a henotheistic people through the time of the Judges, which predates the rise of the monarchy, and throughout the time of the Kingdom of Israel (c.1080-c. 722 BCE). In 931 BCE, following the death of Solomon , the kingdom split in two and a new political entity, the Kingdom of Judah with its capital at Jerusalem , emerged in the south.

The southern kingdom, which consisted of two of the twelve tribes and known as Judah, managed to survive until the year 586 [BCE] when the Babylonians came in and conquered and sent the people into exile. The capital, Jerusalem

importance.justification: The emergence of Judaism established ethical monotheism, shaping Christianity, Islam, and the foundational religious and legal heritage of Western and Near Eastern civilizations.

reviewer_note: There is no agreed moment when Israelite religion became Judaism. The dates mark the monarchy and the exile, and later stages are in the Hebrew Bible record.
